answer:
**Early stopping limits how far optimization follows the training data.** A model often learns broad signal before fitting idiosyncratic noise. Select a checkpoint using validation performance and stop when further updates cease to improve that criterion meaningfully. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

In quadratic linear regression, gradient descent learns high-curvature directions faster than low-curvature directions. Stopping after finitely many steps leaves some directions more strongly shrunk. Ridge also shrinks directions according to the design matrix's spectrum, which explains the regularization analogy.

**The analogy is not exact equality.** With eigenvalue lambda and step size eta, a finite-step filter involves $1-(1-\eta\lambda)^t$, while ridge uses a factor like $\lambda/(\lambda+\alpha)$. One scalar ridge penalty generally cannot match the early-stopping filter at every eigenvalue.

For neural networks the relationship is less direct. Save the best validation checkpoint rather than simply the last step after patience expires. Keep the final test set untouched, and account for noisy validation metrics. Early stopping is a useful control on optimization and generalization, not a theorem that every stopped model equals an L2-penalized fit.

**Technical details and references.**

Early stopping chooses a checkpoint before optimization fully fits noise, using a separate validation criterion and patience rule. For quadratic linear regression, finite gradient-descent time shrinks slowly learned low-curvature directions, resembling spectral regularization. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

It is **not generally exactly equivalent** to ridge with one scalar penalty: early-stopping and ridge apply different spectral filters. In neural networks the connection is even less exact. Save the best checkpoint rather than the last patience-expired one, and avoid repeatedly tuning against the final test set. Compare compute, validation uncertainty, and metric alignment when deciding when to stop.
